on a piece of legislation in this House, I do not think we should adjourn the committee and go to the telephone and ask a certain party whether he is willing to act or not.

The minister could get an
answer between six and eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I will do this, which will
show the hon. member what an open mind and an impartial spirit I am bringing into this resolution. Let the resolution pass and I will try to draft a clause in the bill which will meet the wishes expressed by my hon. friend. I am not saying that Sir Arthur Currie is willing to act as such trustee or as head of such board, I cannot, of course, undertake to pledge myself as regards Sir Arthur Currie. If he is willing to act, I am willing to ask him. If I say here as a minister in charge of a bill that if this becomes legislation I shall ask Sir Arthur Currie to be head of the board of trustees, I think that should be sufficient for my hon. friend. Would anybody doubt my word in this regard.
Does the minister approve the suggestion that two members be named by the Dominion Veterans' Alliance?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no objection at all to receive a suggestion from them.
And as the hon. member for Buirard (Mr. Clark) has suggested, to leave the appointment of the third to those two gentlemen?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: And if they cannot agree, the appointment of the third to be left to the Governor in Council. I am quite willing.
We are not in any way desiring to obstruct this legislation, so that if the minister thinks we are, he is drawing a wrong conclusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am not.

The minister asks us to let the resolution go through. It is now half past five and we have many things to discuss in regard to this resolution. Therefore, I am sure the minister does not expect that the resolution will pass before six o'clock. Let us think of these things between six o'clock and eight. I would not doubt the minister's remark that he would be willing to draft a clause in the bill, but I would want to think over the whole scheme before absolutely concurring in his statement. As it is now half past five, there is no reason why we should decide absolutely upon that point now. Might I read some of the remarks of Sir Arthur Currie which are contained in one
of his letters to the Prime Minister of May 7, 1923. This deals with both aspects of the case as suggested by myself, so that I do not claim any originality in the matter. This is a letter which is in the return brought down the other day. Sir Arthur Currie says, speaking of the adjustment bureau:
I am firmly convinced that such an organization i* desirable and necessary and Mr. MacNeil informs me that the Hon. Dr. Beland and yourself-
This is to the Prime Minister.
-hold similar views. I believe myself that such a service is a proper charge upon government funds and its maintenance could be justified to the members of the House. On the other hand, I do not believe it would be wise for the government to organize directly this proposed service, because if it did the service would soon become as bureaucratic as any other government organization and its decisions would not be as acceptably received as if the members of the organization constituting the service were entirely removed from government control.
This is absolutely along the lines mentioned. He continues:
I suggested to Mr. MacNeil to put before you the idea of creating a small board of some three or four members who would not be .paid for their services but who would be responsible for engaging the members of the adjustment service board or the advocates board, or whatever else you might call it. I, myself, would be glad to serve on such a board.
You have it on record that Sir Arthur Currie would be willing to act.
And I suggest that men like Major-General J. H. MacBrien, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., Major W. H. Her-ridge, D.S.O., and almost anyone else you care tc have, would constitute a suitable committee. This committee could arrange with the G.W.V.A. headquarters, or with certain members of it, to do the necessary work.
He goes on to discuss the financial arrangements. I read this to show that Sir Arthur Currie, who no doubt has the confidence of all classes in this country irrespective of his politics, is entirely of the same opinion that some of us have expressed here. In fact I rather think that idea came from Sir Arthur Currie because I read it before I expressed these views. It appears to me to be a very wise precaution, and I give the minister credit for being as anxious to make this nonpolitical as the rest of us are. There is no desire on the part of any of us to get kudos or advertising in connection with the soldiers or anybody else, but there is in the minds of all hon. members a desire to have this fund handled in such a manner that it will give the soldiers and their dependents every service and at the same time, not be manipulated by the government or the opposition or the Progressive party or any other group in this House. That is my whole intention in offering the suggestion. As regards the proposal of the minister, I would ask him to
14S8
Canteen Funds

allow us to discuss other phases of the matter and let the discussion of this particular phase stand over until after supper. I do not see the difficulties in the matter that the minister puts forward. For example, he says that if two trustees are appointed, they assuredly will not decide upon a third; that one will want one man and another another man. I do not believe that is a correct statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I said that they might.

I understand. I do not
think that is a correct statement, because, as a matter of fact, we have good evidence that again and again in much more difficult matters to handle than this fund, this procedure has been undertaken and carried out. For instance, in the Lemieux Act which orders that conciliation, in certain cases of strikes be attempted, I think it is the law according to that act that one of the conciliators be appointed by the men, the second by the employer, the third to be appointed by the two; or in case of these two failing to agree, the Minister of Labour appoints the third.
I would be willing to agree to the appointment of two men, one by parliament and one by the Dominion Veterans' Alliance, and if these two could not agree on the appointment of the third man- then I would not object to allowing the minister or the Governor in Council to name that one. I do not want the minister to think that there is any desire on our part to hold the matter up on that account, but I would suggest that we allow the question to stand until after eight o'clock and in the meantime discuss other sections.

The resolution differs in
section (2) from the Ralston report, although in all other respects the two are identical. The Ralston report provides that the sum of $100,000 is to be paid to a central board of three trustees, at least two of whom have had overseas service. The resolution omits this proviso; there is no reference to those words, "at least two of whom have had overseas service."

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The hon. member will remember that last year there was a clause in the bill relating to that very point. This is a resolution we have under consideration, but the bill I have before me based upon it contains a clause providing that the majority of the board shall consist of ex-service men.

That is the first point.
The other point I think is even more important. The Ralston report provides specifically that the amount is to be used "by the 
central board of trustees" from time to time, in such amounts and in such manner as it may deem best, for the maintenance and assistance of an adjustment service and bureau for the benefit of ex-service men and their dependents. The resolution as submitted reads:
The sum of $100,000 to be paid to a central board of three trustees appointed by the Governor in Council, without remuneration, etc.
The point I make is this. It is all important in this piece of legislation that the board be as far as possible detached from any government-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We agree.
Mr. L.ADNER: -so as to avoid the possibility of bureaucratic domination which it is thought sometimes exists in government departments, although the belief is not always warranted. The success of the adjustment bureau conducted by the Great War Veterans' Association has been attributable largely to the confidence placed by the soldier body at large in that organization, in the conviction that it was not influenced nor dominated by either governments or governmental departments. As there seems to be a difference between the resolution and the report, I would ask the minister whether in his opinion the principle is that the money is to be used by the central board of trustees from time to time as they see fit and not as the Governor in Council may see fit.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am not supposed to say
in advance what the bill contains but I will read the section of the bill relating to this matter, which as the hon. member will see is word for word what he has suggested:
Tile sum of $100,000 shall be allotted and paid to the central board of trustees to be expended by such board from time to time in such amounts and in such manner as it may deem best for the maintenance and assistance of an adjustment service and bureau at Ottawa for the benefit of ex-members of the forces and their dependents.

I presume there are no
other clauses in the bill which would abrogate the principle that the central board of trustees is to control.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Absolutely none.
I bring this to the attention of the minister because the resolution omits the words, which are so clearly stated in the Ralston report, that the sum is to be used by the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that the resolution is only a general review of what the bill will contain.

Canteen Funds
But the resolution on other points, take for example section (3), is identical with the report.

With all the money that
we are spending on the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and on our appeal boards here, there and everywhere, it seems to me unfortunate that we should find it necessary to take this $100,000 and put it in the hands of either a central or an intermediate board for distribution. To my mind this does not permit of the money accruing directly to the ex-service men. We all agree that this money must be distributed, but as to the establishment of a board for its distribution, that is another matter. Section (2) of the resolution provides that the money is to be paid to the central board-
To be used in such amounts and such manner as it may deem best for the maintenance and assistance of an adjustment service and bureau for the benefit of ex-service men and their dependents.
I think that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment together with its branches is the institution that should function in this matter, and some other method should have been devised for distributing the money than handing over to a board $100,000 belonging to the ex-service men. I want to put on record for the information of the government two or three telegrams representing the feeling of some of my constituents in this regard, and it will be seen that their ideas are not entirely in accord with those expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) and by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark). I represent in this House 110,000 people and my constituency, which covers an area of 30 square miles, embraces centres of population one within a mile of the other, where there are organizations of returned men which exist for the purpose of looking after the dependents and widows of soldiers, as well as taking care of cases of distress. Some of these organizations call themselves Great War Veterans while others are known as returned men's clubs, veterans' clubs, and so on. I did not know that this matter was coming up or I could have been prepared with the facts in this regard. Speaking offhand, however, I may say that there are some seven different clubhouses in my district, one of which was honoured by His Excellency the Governor General who performed the ceremony of turning the key in the lock when the clubhouse was opened, another clubhouse His Excellency honoured by allowing his name to be used in christening it, and it is now known as the Byng Memorial Hall. I have heard it said, and I have seen
it stated in the press that in these clubhouses perhaps a little personal or political strife is stirred up, but I would point to what they have achieved in the last few years and what they will continue to achieve-the taking care of cases of distress which would otherwise be neglected. When I place on Hansard what they say I want hon. members to consider that the messages are from men in the different communities who are trying to do their part as they see it. The first is dated February 27, and is from the Riverdale Great War Veterans' Association, 453 Broadview Avenue, Toronto, an institution whidh possesses assets worth perhaps $20,000 in the form of a modem clubhouse, and looks after upwards of five or six thousand returned men and their dependents. The president says:
Government should retain canteen funds and interest intact. Veterans' Alliance not now recognized by Ontario command G.W.V.A. Kindly convey this information to your Toronto colleagues.
Davidson,
President.
Here is another message from the same branch saying:
Please strenuously oppose grant of one hundred thousand dollars from veterans' canteen funds to Veterans' Alliance.
The next is dated March 16, and is from the Beaches branch of the G.W.V.A., Toronto, which is in a thickly populated district and looks after the interests of about four thousand returned men and their dependents:
Beaches branch G.W.V.A. strongly opposed to Veterans' Alliance application for one hundred thousand dollars from canteen funds to be used in operating a service bureau in Ottawa.
Alexander Magee,
Secretary.
Then the East Toronto branch of the G.W. V.A., which owns a property valued at between $5,000 and $6,000, and serves a community of upwards of one thousand returned men and their dependents, sends me this message:
Strongly protest government action regarding grant of canteen fund to Dominion Veterans' Alliance. Stand by us.
Another message under date of February 27, is from Mr. Shields, I think the secretary of the Toronto and district command. He says:
Our contention is that canteen money should not be used for any organization that does not represent the returned soldiers.
My last message, Mr. Chairman, is from the Scarborough Returned Men's Club, and is dated March 13, 1925:
At a special meeting at the hall, BirchcliSe Heights, on March 13, a resolution was passed strongly protesting against the proposed grant of $100,000 by the Dominion government to the \ eterans' Alliance from
Canteen Funds

the canteen fund. We as veterans at a joint meeting think that the money belongs to the returned men and not to the government, and should not be spent otherwise unless sanctioned by the ex-service men as a whole in the Dominion. We trust you will do all in your power to avoid this action being taken.
I concede, Mr. Chairman, that these wires may not be drafted to meet the wording of the resolution, as I note that the government do not propose to grant the fund to the Veterans' Alliance, but I merely put these messages on record so the minister will have them as a guide in this connection. Before taking my seat, let me again emphasize what is uppermost m my mind, that surely the government has some body which would have the confidence of all sections of the House and which would not appear to be in any way political, even if it was appointed by the hon. minister, so that it would not be necessary to spend some of this money to appoint an intermediate bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend, what he suggests is exactly the proposal to which my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Manion) and my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) take exception. If I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Harris) aright, he suggested that this $100,000 should be disposed of through some government agency-some department or some branch of the public service.

He suggested that, but
the telegrams did not. The telegrams are in accord with what we suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am dealing with the
remarks of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Harris). I do not agree with him that the government should dispose of the money direct. As a matter of principle I agree with my hon. friend from Rainy River, that it should be handed over to a board which is absolutely beyond governmental influence in every province as in Ottawa. That is the idea, and if the bill can be shaped to make that more certain than it is now, I am quite willing to accept any suggestion to that end.
Is it not possible to supply this $100,000 from government funds instead of taking it from the canteen funds?

I think the minister
will recognize that the general principle governing the Canteen funds is that those funds are the property of the men. That being so, is he following out the principle in allocating $100,000 of the funds for the establishment of a bureau? If such a bureau is essential in the interests of the men to look after their pension and other interests, then the expense

of its establishment comes fairly under governmental expenditure. To meet the expenses of the bureau out of funds belonging to the men I do not think is justified. Under the circumstances I should be glad to have the opinion of the minister on the point I have raised, namely, whether a portion of certain funds belonging to the men should be taken to establish a bureau the expenses in connection with which I think should properly be met by the government. We have had brought to our notice a number of objections raised by returned men in one part of the country regarding the proposal to set aside this $100,000 from the canteen funds. Perhaps the minister will inform us whether he has received similar protests. My view is that we are departing from the principle of regarding this money as the property of the men if we take a portion of it for the purpose of establishing a bureau. If that bureau is necessary, then I think the cost of it should be a governmental charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I regard the adjustment
bureau as a very useful agency. It affords the men a good deal more satisfaction to deal with the department or with the pension board through an agency of their own. Up to the present, aside from certain assistance given by the former government and! this government to some of the returned men's associations, these duties have been carried out by the associations at the expense of the men. The recommendation of the royal commission that $100,000 of the canteen fund be set aside for the purposes of an adjustment bureau is animated by the same spirit as that in which my hon. friend's remarks are made, because the men will to that extent be relieved from contributing toward the maintenance of the bureau. This recommendation was made by the royal commission after an investigation extending over a year, during which they went into the whole problem and obtained the views of returned men from one end of the country to the other. I believe it is a proper recommendation. Indeed, I submitted it last year and I think the House unanimously agreed that it was a proper course to follow.
Not unanimously.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Well, I did not hear any
strenuous objection last year. The hon. member says he did not agree, but I understood that the resolution and the bill based upon it were adopted unanimously by the House. At all events I think the recommendation is a good one. As to the board of trustees, if some suggestion can be offered by which this

Private Bills
board will be made entirely independent of government control, I shall be willing to accept it.

Before six o'clock is called,
may I remind the minister that considerable information was requested at the last sitting of the committee and that it might be useful to have that information here after dinner?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Is it with regard to the
disablement cheques? These have been produced.
Laid on the table?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think so, yes.
There were other questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think all the information has been tabled.

I would like to
ask if the Minister of Justice has Looked into these bills to see if public rights are safeguarded.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When these bills were
before the committee the other day, I think my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) took some objection, and when I came into the House he asked me to consult with the officers of the crown as to the legality of the things which are asked by these bills. I confess I have not had time myself to look into the bids, but I have submitted them to the officers of my department, this one and the one fathered by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and they have reported to me that no public interest was being adversely affected by them.

Th,at is the
very information I wanted. I am willing to take the minister's statement in that respect.
Private Bills

As I understand it, the
enacting clauses of both these bills that have been under discussion have been entirely stricken out in the Private Bills committee and new enacting clauses inserted in lieu thereof. We have not these amendments before us, and with all due respect to the chairman he is not the best reader in the world, and I must confess that what he read conveyed very little if anything to me. It seems to me these bills ought first to be reprinted if we are to know anything about what is being done. I do not think I could give an intelligent explanation of a single sentence the chairman read; perhaps that is my fault.
Mr.. MeGIVERIN: There may be a good deal in what my hon. friend says about having the bills reprinted. The point in connection with both these bills is that originally the promoters asked the committee to decide that the patent should be reinstated. But what the committee did was this:	In both these

The people who appeared before my committee stated that they had overlooked this, and as well the provision that they could apply to the Commissioner of Patents, and what the committee did was to amend the bills and give these people power to appear before the Commissioner of Patents and to state their case, and he sitting as a judge, would decide whether any other rights were being interfered with. I do not know whether
I am entitled to speak again on this bill, because this is the second reading, and I spoke the other night. I asked the Minister of Justice if he would look into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have had the officers of the Department of Justice look into the bill and they report that perhaps this bill would not be necessary because they think the patent is still in existence, and yet on the other hand they do not see that any public interest is adversely affected by the bill.

The point I raised when I objected the other day was this: apparently the Patent Commissioner has granted a patent and declares that it is all in order and he is satisfied under the general statute. speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed in committee consideration of a proposed resolution with regard to the distribution of canteen funds.-Mr. Beland -Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Has the minister taken any steps to obtain the opinion of the Great War Veterans on this proposition?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I explained before six
o'clock that the opinion of the ex-service men had been obtained by the royal commission during their peregrinations through the country, and the resolution and bill are the result of the recommendations of that committee. As a matter of fact they are an exact reproduction of the recommendation.

I grant all that,
but the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) read a telegram stating that the veterans in many of their headquarters did object to this legislation. Has the minister heard any objections to this legislation from the war veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I have received also a
number of despatches asking me not to allot one hundred thousand dollars to one particular organization. In some cases the G.W.V.A. were mentioned as not being agreeable to it. In some other matters the Dominion Veterans' Alliance was mentioned, but ,a delegation met some members of the government a few days ago and they submitted to members of the government that they were in favour of the resolution as introduced in this House this year and also of that of last year. The delegation was quite representative.
Of what organizations?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Great War Veterans'
Association, the Tubercular Veterans' Association.

The Grand Army of
United Veterans and the Amputation Association?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not know that the
Grand Army of United Veterans were represented, but I received a letter from their secretary stating that they endorsed the resolution as introduced.

Were representatives of the
Army and Navy Veterans there?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They were not, but I had a long interview with their president, Mr. Brown, if 1 mistake not, when he explained to me that the desire of veterans' organizations in general should be secured before any appointment of the central board of trustees was made, and I agreed to that. It is my intention to consult the different organizations, and if they agree upon one association such as the Dominion Veterans' Alliance, to consult the Dominion Veterans' Alliance as to who would be an acceptable candidate for a member of the central board of trustees. This afternoon before six o'clock the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) read a despatch from Mr. Shields. I have before me the name of Mr. Shields as being one of the representatives on this delegation which endorsed the legislation. Whether it is the same Mr. Shields or not, I cannot say. Generally speaking, I would say that the legislation is acceptable to the returned mien.

Apart from individual
associations, has the minister received many telegrams from large organizations protesting against this $100,000 distribution that he speaks of, or are the protests just from local centres? Has he received any wide-spread protests?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No wide-spread protests.

Could the minister give
us a rough idea of the different organizations from -which he has received protests, so that we may know? I have received a few, not many.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
So far as I know, there
was no protest against this legislation being introduced for the distribution. The protest was against the apportionment of a sum of money to one particular association.
Exactly, but how widespread was the protest?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think it was mainly confined to Toronto and Ontario, not very much outside of that. If my hon. friend insists, I may give him the names of the members of the delegation.

No. I saw the names
and I saw some of the members of the delegation which waited upon the minister. They
Canteen Funds

laid the memorandum before me and other hon. members. They were agreeable, but they comprise only the members of the Great War Veterans' Association and the Tubercular Veterans' Association. No others signed the memorandum, and I was curious to know if there was any wide-spread opposition outside of that expressed in telegrams from local organizations. If the minister has a list of them, I would be glad if he would tel us what he has in the way of protests.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There is no such protest
as that to which the hon. member refers. The Grand Army of United Veterans, I think, ha3 also wired me, but I presume that they were unaware of the exact content of the resolution or the manner in which this apportionment of $100,000 was going to be made, because within the last week I received a letter -I have not the letter with me, but I can produce it-from the Grand Army of United Veterans endorsing this legislation. As regards the Army and Navy Veterans, I had a conversation with their president, Mr. Brown.
The Amputation Association?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have not heard either way from them. I do not think they would have any objection to it.

Coming as I do from a soldier city, I have quite a number of returned soldiers in my constituency including those at the Christie street hospital and a great deal of objection is expressed to the distribution of this fund as proposed in the resolution now before the committee. I sympathize with the minister. He has a most difficult task to perform in administering the distribution of the canteen fund. There are many ways in which this can be divided, and it may be almost impossible to please everybody. I understand that one has to be reasonable in the matter; in fact, there is only one other fund that one must be more careful about, and that is the campaign fund, if there be such a thing. I have received many protests from soldier organizations in Toronto, and I will read one from the Toronto and York County District Command of the Great War Veterans' Association. I have known Mr. Bray, the president, for many years, and I have found him a very reasonable and sensible soldier who would not want to give anyone any trouble. The record he has is that he has co-operated with the civic authorities to the best of his ability. He objects to this proposition and he has reasonable grounds for doing so. The sol-

diers of Toronto do not want to give the government any trouble and they want to help the minister and the department. They know the minister has been zealous in his work and that he is not responsible for mistakes that have been made in the past. The Toronto and York County District Command embraces all the district of Toronto and York and they are very much opposed to this division. I have a number of telegrams, but I will read only this one:
Legislation in connection with canteen funds coining before the House to-day (Thursday) provide for the setting aside of one hundred thousand dollars from the canteen funds for the purpose of setting up veteran service bureau in Ottawa under the Dominion Veterans' Alliance. Toronto and York County District Command, Great War Veterans' Association, absolutely opposed to setting aside any moneys from the canteen fund which belongs to all ex-soldiers to the Veterans' Alliance. Veterans' Alliance is only paper organization and does not represent organized ex-soldiers. Toronto and district and the Ontario provincial command withdrew from Veterans' Alliance eight months ago. Suggest you make this known in the House when legislation is brought forward particularly the fact that we are opposed to setting aside of any moneys from the canteen fund to the Veterans' Alliance.
I know President Bray and the officers of this organization, and I am aware how they worked with the civic authorities during last winter when there was a great deal of distress among the returned men in Toronto. These men gave a great deal of service not only to the soldiers, but to the citizens at large that were in distress, and also to ex-soldiers from the Old Country who were in difficulties. As I say this telegram is from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Who sent this last despatch which the hon. member has read?

It is signed by Harry
Bray, president, and Alexander Shields, secretary.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I see it is dated February 25. Later than this date, both gentlemen appeared before me and endorsed this legislation.

If the minister will come up to Toronto he will still find a lot of opposition-I was at a meeting of soldiers and they were all opposed to this legislation. The city of Toronto found it necessary to maintain a bureau of its own owing to the fact that the soldiers had found it impossible to obtain any relief from the department at Ottawa. They went to the city hall and applied for assistance and the city, at the expense of the tax-payers at large, was obliged to maintain a bureau of its own. There is such a vast amount of red tape in connection with the pension board that when the returned men, of the city of

Canteen Funds
Toronto at any rate-and I am able to speak particularly of them-endeavoured to secure some relief they encountered all sorts of obstacles in the shape of one technicality after another. There is also in Toronto the Ontario Soldiers' Aid Commission. It costs a lot of money, and I know for a fact that there are agencies of this commission in Hamilton, London and other places.
Now, I do not say that the minister i3 altogether to blame; as I observed in my opening remarks, I am quite aware that he has a difficult fund to handle, and even though he might devise ten or fifteen different ways of administering it, it is possible that there would still be dissatisfaction. The fact remains nevertheless that a considerable number of men in the city of Toronto are out of work and in a critical condition and something must be done to assist them. It was said the other night by Mr. Shields of the G.W.V.A., that 60 per cent of the men out of work in Toronto were returned1 men, and a large percentage of them do not come under the pension law as it is to-day. I recognize, of course, as everybody does, that this government, in common with its predecessors, has done a great deal for the returned men. There is no doubt about that. And I know also that there is nothing partisan at all about this question, for all parties are anxious to see the right thing done by the veterans. I do not believe that anyone has the interests of the veterans more at heart than the minister himself (Mr. Beland). There is another organization located in the riding of East Toronto, and I know that the hon. member who represents that district (Mr. Ryckman) has taken a great deal of interest in the situation there. Indeed, I do not know of anyone who has been more diligent in the endeavour to further the interests of the men than that hon. member lias been. And this organization and others as well are all opposed to the assigning of this $100,000 to a central board for distribution. I have here a telegram from Riverdale branch of the Great War Veterans' Association, to the following effect:
T. L. Church, M.P.,
Parliament Building,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Please strenuously oppose grant of $100,000 from veterans' canteen funds to Veterans' Alliance. Thanks.
And the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) read a number of telegrams this afternoon from various units on the same question.
I criticize the assigning of this $190,000 to the board on this ground, that the government is under no necessity so far as I can see of entrusting the fund to such a body. That fund in my opinion should be administered 96

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
without cost to the soldiers. Surely in view of the fact that we have a department to look after the re-establishment of soldiers some means could have been devised of administering this fund without cost to the men. I do not go so far as to say that there has been any diversion of the fund, but I do strongly maintain that the government could have discovered some way of administering it without cost to the general body of returned men. I believe that if the minister had asked the House to vote $20,000 in his estimates for this purpose that vote would have carried; for if there is one fund more than another that should be administered free of cost to the returned men it is this one. I know of course that the minister is trying to effect economies, but it seems to me that in this particular department great care should be taken to see that whatever saving is made shall not be at the expense of the returned men.
I criticize the proposal on another ground: in handing over the $100,000 to this board the government is simply duplicating the work that is being carried on. I know of my own experience that such duplication does exist. For example, I know of a soldier who made application to five or six different persons for relief; he went first to the local district, and was referred to some other authority, and from that body he went to another, and so on. So that there is no question to my mind at least as to the existence of an expensive duplication; and when this board is charged with administering the fund this evil will only be aggravated.
As to handing over $50,000 to the American Red Cross, I do not know that we are going to do very much good. There are certainly a number of our returned men out of work in the United States, but my suggestion to the government would be to provide some general scheme of repatriation which would enable these men to come back to Canada. There are hundreds of them out of work in Detroit and other American cities and they are not likely to get work inasmuch as, before the American authorities will allow them to take any job, they must swear allegiance to the government of the United States. And returned Canadian soldiers after fighting for their king and flag will do no such thing. I would point out to the minister that after the Civil War in the United States the men of the Grand Army of the Republic did not have to leave that country to find employment, nor did they have to apply to any British organization such as the Red Cross, which did not then exist, for relief. They

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Canteen Funds

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
did not have to go the government of a foreign country to look for help. I have a number of letters from returned Canadian soldiers telling of distress in the United States and many of them are unable to get work owing to the fact that they will not take the oath to a foreign flag. In my opinion this $50,000 should be placed under the control of the minister himself; I believe in responsible ministers discharging such duties as properly appertain to their office. It seems to me that it is unwise to hand over $100,060 to this province, $75,000 to another province, and so on, on the basis of the number of returned men resident in these places respectively. I think it would be far better for the minister himself to control the administration of the money under section (4) of the resolution; as the resolution stands the government simply divests itself of all control and leaves the matter subject to conflicting regulations in the various provinces. But where does the returned man come in on this thing? There should have been a vote on the proposition by provinces according to the military districts. What is the general officer in command of the district for? He knows the number of pensioners that are in his district and he ought to be able to give some idea to the minister as to how these moneys might be distributed under this section. We have a Department of National Defence, we have a Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and we have local district commands with headquarters; and as I say, the general officer commanding the district knows just who his men are. On the whole, therefore, it would have been better to leave the matter to the minister. I am not here to criticize the minister, because my wish is to co-operate with him in every way possible. But one cannot help referring to these things. Again, what about the Amputation Association? I do not see any reference in this resolution to that large association. And what about the blind1 soldiers? And then there is the question of unemployment, which is a very serious matter among the returned men. I think that a great many of the soldiers, in the city from which I come at any rate, would rather see the recommendations of the Ralston report carried out, one of which provides for scholarships to promising children of ex-service men. I know of one case in which the father was killed, and the mother having died, the orphans were left with an aunt. This lady is trying her best to send two of them to high school and then to university, but her application for a pension for these children of 
sixteen and seventeen was denied. No doubt if the soldier-father had returned he would have given his children the best possible education within his power, and I think this is an excellent recommendation by the Ralston commission. Indeed, if the minister bad administered the fund along the lines of the Ralston report I think he would have followed' a very sensible course, because the commission took the views of soldiers all over the country and the recommendations contained in their report are doubtless founded on a consideration of those views. Coming from a city where there are large numbers of soldiers in distress, I sympathize with the minister in his endeavours to do all he can for the returned men, but I say to him now that the distribution of this fund as proposed is going to cause a lot of dissatisfaction among those interested. From my knowledge of the distress among many returned men in Toronto and elsewhere I believe one of the best uses to which this fund could be put would be to relieve that distress by way of finding the men employment or granting them financial assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

speechtext: Is there a reciprocal arrangement on the part of the United States?
No.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not know that in the United States they have any canteen fund to distribute. Perhaps my hon. friend knows.

If they have not
a canteen fund they should have one.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
If they have such a fund
I think they should alllot to the Canadian Red Cross a certain amount for the benefit of American returned men living in Canada. Now, my hon. friend from North Toronto suggested to me that the opinion of the returned men throughout Canada should be secured as to the proper distribution of the canteen fund. We all agree on that. The former government, led by my right hon. friend who now leads the opposition (Mr. Meighen), passed an order in council on November 3, 1921, creating a committee which was known as the canteen fund disposal committee. The order in council recites that the opinion of all returned men in Canada should be obtained as to the proper disposal of the canteen fund. This committee issued a circular or ballot containing a number of questions, and through the post offices, the soldiers' hospitals and other agencies, over 500,000 of these were distributed among the returned men. The number of ballots received expressing an opinion as to the disposal of the fund was only
22.000	out of a possible total of 450,000 soldiers in Canada, therefore it was decided that owing to the relatively small number of opinions expressed the government would not be justified in taking any action. This was shortly after the present government came into office; I think it was in February, 1922. It was represented to me by the men who composed this committee, appointed by order in council under the former government, that in view of the fact that no one opinion had more than
5.000	supporters it would be inadvisable to proceed on that basis. The whole question was subsequently placed before the royal commission, the members of which would find it a relatively easy matter to secure the opinions of the men all over the country. They did that; they have made their report, and they
Canteen Funds

have recommended the distribution of the fund as proposed last year and again this year. The hon. member (Mr. Church), who is a personal friend of mine, says he is willing to leave the matter with me; that he would rather have the distribution of the funds placed in the hands of the minister. I thank him for his good intentions, but even if the whole House were willing to leave it to me I should refuse to accept the task, because I understand it is a most difficult one. The method that has been adopted is one that will give the greatest satisfaction to the greatest number, though I admit there will still be dissatisfaction.
So far as the central board of trustees is concerned, I repeat that since his name has been brought into the discussion this afternoon I am disposed to ask Sir Arthur Currie to be head of this board of trustees. I am willing also to take the suggestion of the soldiers' organizations, omitting none^ as to a second member of the board. With regard to the third member I do not know to whom I should have recourse, but I think that could be left to the minister or to the government. On that point I may say that I have not heard a single word of complaint with regard to the personnel of the royal commission which I appointed. They were three returned men who commanded the respect and confidence of every soldier in Canada, and in this instance my only desire would be to act in the best interests of the returned men. I am also disposed to ask the board to obtain the opinion of the returned men as to who should be in charge of this office for which provision is being made. It is not for me to say it will be the Great War Veterans' Association, the Army and Navy Veterans, The Grand Army of United Veterans, The Dominion Veterans' Alliance, or the Tubercular Veterans Association. That is not for me to say, and I do not intend to say it. All I 9 p.m. want to do is to request this board to refund to the disablement fund the 815,000 which has been advanced from that fund for the maintenance of the bureau. This bureau has been carried on by The Great War Veterans' Association-for some time as the Great War Veterans' Association, some time as the Dominion Veterans Alliance. I am not conversant with all the details of the functionings of these two associations. It is claimed' that the Dominion Veterans' Alliance represents all the associations; some say it does not. I do know that Mr. MacNeil has from the day I came back from the Old Country been in charge of the soldiers' interests before every par-

liamentary committee, has had to do with the preparation of legislation and has generally represented them in all matters affecting their welfare. I think everybody will agree that he has discharged those duties to the satisfaction of all concerned. But if he is not the man it will be for the central board of trustees, not for me or the members of the government to decide.
I say in all sincerity that a board of trustees consisting of three members will be appointed if the bill to be based on this resolution becomes law. Deducting then, the $15,000 which they will be requested to refund to the disablement fund, they may administer the balance of that money, $85,000, as they deem best. We have spent a good many hours upon this resolution and I hardly think the objections urged have been such as to warrant so lengthy a discussion. I am pleased, nevertheless that the discussion has taken place. I suggest that the committee now adopt the resolution in order that we may advance the legislation one step. When the bill is under consideration I shall have a few amendments to propose-I shall not say to correct some defects, but rather to make some changes based upon suggestions offered by hon. gentlemen opposite.

Section 1 of the resolution refers to the payment of outstanding accounts. I understand that this money is in the hands of the Receiver General and I can hardly understand that there could; be any outstanding expenses in connection with it. Will the minister explain the nature of these outstanding accounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Last year when the resolution was before the House I remember giving an explanation on this point. I have not the reference before me at the moment, but in short it means that some accounts are outstanding against the fund for certain regimental units which have been disbanded. This sum is set aside at the request of the Minister of National Defence in order to provide for any outstanding accounts that might be presented against the fund. My hon. friend will find that the bill provides that if after four years all claims that have been presented have been paid, if there is a balance left, that balance shall fall into the general fund which is to be allotted to the different provinces. We have nothing to do with that.

But should not that have been ascertained during the last year? What my hon. friend speaks of now is the condition

Canteen Funds
that obtained a year ago in expectation of the bill passing. The bill did not pass. A year now has elapsed, and surely any outstanding accounts could have been ascertained in the period of a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I would not say definitely, but I am informed that small accounts have been paid even during the past twelve months. It is a measure of prudence only, and it is not done at my request or suggestion.
Mr. RO'SS (Kingston):	I should like to
say a few words on this proposal before it passes the committee. There seems to have been a change in the situation lately, because there certainly was a great deal of opposition amongst the returned men in regard to this section of the government's proposal, but within the last week that opposition seems to have faded away. Certain men have oome here to Ottawa, and without any consultation with the members to whom telegrams were sent, consent has been given to this proposal, so we are informed by the minister. Now it would seem only natural that the service men who sent these telegrams should have conferred with the members to whom they were sent, if such approbation of the government's proposal has been obtained as the minister now suggests.
To what is the opposition due in regard to this matter? When the termination of the war was in sight, or immediately after, it was determined that the welfare and the interests of the returned men. should not be left to a government department. One would naturally expect that the Militia department might have carried on that work, but it was proposed that a separate department should be created which would be composed of laymen, and would be, as it were, friendly towards the returned men. That organization was created, and became the immense organization we now know as the DjS.C.R., of which the minister is the head, and he should have at least something to say in regard to its administration. We all know how friendly and how genial he is. You have only to approach him vo get a promise that everything will be set right, but then he suddenly bucks up against one of these iron-clad officials of his, his back weakens, and the returned soldiers are forgotten. Consequently the very department that was supposed to have sympathy for the returned men has become, one might almost say, their deadly enemy. Every member of this House knows how little sympathy he gets when he approaches that department in regard to a returned man. They will do nothing but carry out the strict letter of the
law; sympathy they know little about. The result is that the returned man, instead of placing his whole case in their hands, has turned away from them, feeling that his only safety is outside of that department which should be his friend and sympathizer, and he leaves his case with an organization of this kind.
In the past Mr. MacNeil the secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association has fought this department through thick and thin till he was almost discouraged, but I would like the committee to remember that Mr. MacNeil did not do all the work. Outside of his work, there was the tubercular, amputation and the blind organizations, all with their own administration looking after the needs of their own men. I do not know whether they will be altogether satisfied to see the work taken out of their hands. The committee will readily understand that it requires some years of work to become acquainted with the technical problems coming up in the tubercular, amputation and blind cases, and I do not know that one general board can do that work. That work must be carried on. Whether or not there has been a secret understanding arrived at as to the redistribution of this fund, I do not know. But the fact remains that there was opposition, and I want to say that the proposal here is one that the government itself should take up.
I want to point out my opposition to this proposal. I may be alone in my views; I have not consulted with anyone else. My position is this. The returned man is the ward of the government and of this country, and we cannot get away from that responsibility. There is no use putting that responsibility on some other organization. The returned mam in general is the ward of this country and of the government, I care not what government is in power, and he should get all the sympathy he deserves. I do not know whether the intention of the department now is to shift the-responsibility on to some other body. We now have the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment, the pension board, and the Federal appeal board, and now this other organization is to be started. If it is necessary for the returned men to have such an organization as this to advance their interests and present their case to the government, I think the government should pay for it. It looks to me as if the government has taken 8100,000, to wash its hands of the interests of the returned man and say: We are done. Because in the future they will' say that these cases have to come before this special board that is
Canteen Funds

to be appointed. I do not think this House should lose sight of the fact that the government and parliament and the country at large has to take care of the returned man. The returned men, the sick and disabled *are the wards of the government, and the government should not get away from that responsibility by having this board appointed. If it is necessary for the returned men to go outside the Department of Soldiers Civil-Reestablishment, the government should pay for it, or provide some easier way, grease the way a little bit for the returned men to get the ear of the D.S.C.R. To-day if you go to the minister about a pension or something else affecting the soldiers, he will tell you he cannot do anything, that the pension board is absolutely independent. If you go to the pension board, they will tell you that their reports come from the D.S.C.R. medical men, and that they cannot help themselves; they have to take the D.S.C.R. reports. The thing is so tied up and connected and intermingled [DOT]that the ordinary man cannot distinguish between them, and I do not know that they themselves know which of the medical men are pension men and which are D.SjC.R. men.
Now what are the matters to be taken up by this board? The report says:
There is a variety of instances in connection with such questions as government employment.
Well, this government is not going to have anything to do with unemployment, so that part of the report is washed away. The government is not going to be responsible in any way for unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think that refers to the
.civil service.

I do not see why,
because there is the provision made that the returned men must always get the preference in applying for a civil service position. Is not that a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It is a fact, but still I
think that refers to the civil service.
But still the government does not do it.
First preference at a pick and shovel job.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There may be a disabled
man who will look for some man to present his case before the Civil Service Commission. I think what my hon. friend has read refers to the Civil Service Commission.
But the hon. minister is not sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think so.

The minister is
not sure as to whether they get their preference or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It refers to that.

Thie government
is responsible and should look after them. As I say, the returned1 man is a ward of the government and should be looked after. We have the report in connection with that. This report says:
There are a variety of instances in connection wicn such questions as government employment, land settlement, training, housing, and rehabilitation activities generally, the consideration affecting which depend on the presentation of the individual case rather than on the terms of a general regulation. There are also parliamentary matters not only affecting pensions biu amendments to existing statutes.
And so on. It is most difficult for anyone to look after the interests of the blind and tubercular. I do not know whether the minister has had any information that these people will be looked after, or if there is any understanding between the three or four as-' sociations in regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I know that most of the
representatives of the organizations with whom I have come in contact favour this legislation. The moment they know that no particular organization is going t-o be favoured in the matter of employment in preference to another organization, they are in favour of the legislation. My idea of an employment bureau would be a place where the central board of trustees would consult all the associations; and more than one man is required for a bureau of that kind. I am satisfied that it takes at least five or six or seven men or employees to attend to such a bureau. My idea of the constitution of such a bureau would be that all the associations should have a representative on it, so that everybody would be represented.

So far, so good. That seems to be the opposition the minister heard of from the men who approached him, but at the same time at the beginning, those who put up the opposition, were given to understand that there was no place from where the funds for a bureau could be obtained. They believed the bureau was absolutely necessary, because they believed the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment had fallen down on the job, and there was a want of sympathy. The minister had all the sympathy, but that is as far' as his department went. There was any amount of

Canteen Funds
sympathy with the minister, but he could not get any further. He was not responsible, and the returned men believed that a bureau was necessary, and there was no other money to be obtained for this bureau; therefore rather than see the bureau done away with and the possibility of it being destroyed they said, "Very good, we are willing to take that hundred thousand dollars"; but if there was sympathy in this House for the sentiment that the government should leave every cent of that money to the men who served overseas and who really put the money into the canteen fund, then being in sympathy with them, the government would say, "Very good, we will see that this bureau shall carry on; there is no sympathy with your case in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and therefore we will see that there will be a bureau to carry on, and we will provide the very small amount necessary". When this hundred thousand dollars is disposed of -and it is not going to last very long, as fifteen thousand dollars has gone already- then what? Where will the returned men be then?
They will go to the labour bureau.

I want the House to keep in mind the position of this matter. It looks to me as if the government were saying, "We will Start you off, what the end will be we do not care". After the hundred thousand dollars has been expended there will still be the returned men's case to be considered, unless there is a department more sympathetic than the department is at the present time. There will be the necessity for a bureau, and I think the proper thing now would be for the government to recognize that responsibility, sympathy having failed with the department, and say, "We will carry on the bureau, and meet the small amount of expenditure that would be required". When you can get three big men in this country to take upon themselves the responsibility of the work without any remuneration, then I think the government should be willing to pay for the office administration. That is my objection to this hundred thousand dollar scheme. In the first place, the government has no right to take it for a thing of this kind. The government should support this proposition, as sympathy has failed in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re. establishment; and by voting the hundred thousand dollars you are making no provision for the carrying on of the bureau. That bureau will go on as long as there are
disabled men in the country and that will be for many many years to come.
Mr. MANIO'N: There are still a number of things, I imagine, about the resolution to be debated before we report it because the minister will remember the first day it came up we settled on the disablement fund, and this afternoon and evening we have discussed almost entirely the appointment of the trustees, but there was another matter I brought to the minister's attention upon which he has not made any remark. I will give him credit for his remarks about the trustees. He has certainly, I think, shown a willingness, which I sincerely hope he will live up to, to respond to the proposition made in good part by this side of the House to try to get the trustees appointed in such a manner that they will be above parties and that sort of thing, and will not make of themselves a political board. I was pleased to have him agree that Sir Arthur Currie might be chairman, because I think that is the wish of all those who have taken an interest in this fund. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) in regard to the appointment of a second trustee is also a good one; that is to have the Dominion Veterans' Alliance appoint a second trustee, that alliance being made up of all the different associations in this country.

The Dominion Alliance which has been referred to I understand is doing the work which this board will be doing when it is formed. It may be the desire that this work may be done by the same board. Why ask this Dominion Alliance to appoint a man to the board which will deal with these cases and look after the interests of returned men?

The Dominion Veterans' Alliance is made up, according to my understanding-and I think it is correct-not only of the Great War Veterans' Association, but of all the other war veterans' associations in the country. It is a sort of combination of the Great War Veterans' associations, the Grand Army of United Veterans and all the other associations. I think it would be well to have all the veterans of the country included in this alliance. Not only are the Great War Veterans of this country interested in the canteen fund but all the veterans in Canada are interested in it. I made it my business the other day to look into the figures of the numbers of men belonging to this association. So far as I could get the figures -and frankly I got them from some of the officers of the Great War Veterans' Associa-
Canteen Funds

tion, they showed that something like 215,000 or 220,000 belonged to all the different associations in the country, so that this left around
200,000	returned soldiers who do not belong to any association. The latter are just as much interested in the canteen fund as those who do belong to an association, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree. The figures as given to me the other da5r, a copy of which I now have in my hand, are as follows:
Army and Navy Veterans	 60,000
Grand Army of United Veterans	 600
Tubercular Veterans' Association	 5,000
Amputation Veterans	 3,000
Canadian Legion	 600

According to these figures, 100,000 have gone to the United States, but even they are interested in this canteen fund. The point I wish to make is that all the different soldiers, so far as we can reach them, should have something to say with regard to the appointment of these trustees. While we cannot cal! in the 100,000 soldiers who have gone to the United States to take part in the voting, we can call in the organized veterans' associations of this country, and the proposal of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) is that after Sir Arthur Currie, if he accepts, is appointed, the second1 trustee be appointed by the Dominion Veterans' Association, which includes the different associations of veterans in Canada.

I have received this telegram :
Government should retain canteen funds and interest intact. Veterans' Alliance not now recognized by Ontario Great War Veterans' Association. And in fact is to-day only a paper organization with official seeking own aggrandizement and personal gain. Kindly convey this information to your Toronto colleagues.
Perhaps the hon. member can tell us who they are.

I am glad my hon. friend is trying to help me out so well. I am not married to the idea of the Dominion Veterans' Alliance. The only reason I suggested it was because until recently it was supposed to be an organization made up of a combination of the officers of all the different associations. The telegram which my hon. friend has may be correct, and the Dominion Veterans' Alliance may not be as represented. If it is not and if there be objection to it, the Great War Veterans' Association and these other associations which I have named should be asked to have their officers get together and pick a man. I do not know the Dominion Veterans' Alliance, and I am speaking subject to correction. After the second trustee has been appointed, the suggestion of the hon.

member for Burrard is that the third trustee is to be appointed by the other two. I was pleased to have the minister appear to agree at least with the idea if it can be worked out, and I do not see any reason why it should not be worked out.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) asked why some Other organizations should be requested to assist in appointing a trustee who would be merely picking the present organized adjustment bureau, which is handled altogether by the Great War Veterans' Association. I do not intend to suggest that any strings be tied to the trustees in regard to an appointment. The appointment of the adjustment bureau should be left entirely in the hands of these trustees. I do not mean to suggest that we should insert in the bill a clause stating that the trustees must appoint So-and-so and So-and-so to handle the adjustment bureau. The matter would be entirely in their hands, and after the three trustees met and discussed the matter, if they decided to use the adjustment bureau that is in existence to-day, I have no quarrel with them, and I do not mean to quarrel with the adjustment bureau at all. I hope that whatever appointments are made, those men will look at this as a position of honour and of trust, and that they will carry out their duties without pay, in the same manner that, I think, most of us who are discussing this question are attempting to carry out ours, in other words, entirely for the benefit of the returned soldiers. I admit the minister has been exceedingly reasonable in regard to the appointment of the trustees. Of course the proposition was a fair one, and I do not see how he could have dealt with it otherwise.
Another question that comes up, one which I brought up earlier in the day, is that of the use of $100,000 from the canteen fund in order to carry on this bureau for the next three or four years. Before I touch on that, I must confess I rather think the question was brought up already to-night, but I was going over some correspondence dealing with this matter and I missed the explanation. Will the minister explain again what the $20,000 mentioned in clause 1 is to be used for.

speechtext:
From some of the units that have been disbanded. I understand. I

Canteen Funds
am not in a position to give details about that. This is what I said last year in reply to a question in this connection:
The National Defence department have submitted occasionally to the Finance department small accounts for payment. What these accounts are exactly I am not in a position to say, but I might suggest thst they are accounts from trustees of former regimental units. Be that as it may, these accounts must be passed upon by the National Defence department and approved by the Finance department. As late as 1923 the Finance department had paid out on these accounts an amount of $2,000. The commission recommend-
That is the royal commission.
-that $20,000 be retained for this purpose, and I presume that if any balance should be left of this amount of $20,000 after a certain delay has elapsed, it would ultimately be distributed amongst the provinces on the pro rata scale mentioned.
There is in the bill, not in the resolution, this provision:
The sum of $20,000 shall be held by the Receiver General for Canada for the payment of any outstanding accounts or claims in respect of the units, the funds of which are included in the canteen funds, provided that should any portion of this amount remain unexpended on the 1st day of July 1929, such unexpended portion shall be disposed of as set forth in paragraph (e) of this section.
That is, distributed amongst the different provinces.

I was glad when
this matter was up a few days ago to hear the pronouncement from the minister that he had altered his views in regard to the course that should be pursued in dealing with the share of the canteen fund to which the returned soldiers now in Yukon are entitled. The minister has said repeatedly during this discussion, not only to-day but on the former occasion, that the bill of last year passed the House and committee without protest. Its terms, as he put it, were quite satisfactory to all concerned. Perhaps I personally did not protest strongly enough, but I felt quite sure that I had protested. I should not like it to go out to my friends among the returned soldiers, not only in Yukon but elsewhere, that I had sat in my place and let the bill, as it was last session, go by without protest. Nor would I let the resolution as we have it now pass without voicing my objection to it. I find on consulting Hansard that my remarks were plain enough. On July 14 I asked:
Mr. Black (Yukon): Why is it the allotment for British Columbia and the Yukon are joined? This allotment is not made in accordance with military districts and the percentage returnable to the Yukon can be ascertained as accurately as the percentage returnable for any province. It will be a smaller amount, but why should it be tied up with British Columbia?
Mr. Beland:	It is the recommendation of the royal
commission.
Mr. Black (Yukon):	I protest against that. I
suggest that the exact percentage due to the Yukon be ascertained and allotted to the Yukon to be distributed by a local committee there, altogether separato and apart from British Columbia. Is it possible to do that? I submit there is no more reason why Yukon should be attached to British Columbia for this purpose than that Yukon should be attached to Prince Edward Island.
That is a plain protest but it was entirely disregarded, and I find I protested again on July 16, a few days later. Since then I have taken occasion to correspond with Colonel J. L. Ralston, the chairman of the Ralston commission, and I have discovered in that correspondence the basis on which these percentages of allotment are calculated. I endeavoured to get the information from ;he minister last session but I must confess I could not do it. Having got it from Colonel Ralston, however, I find it is quite simple to make the Yukon calculation. Colonel Ralston in a letter to me on November 22 last says
The total percentage fixed by our report for distribution to British Columbia and the Yukon Territory is 10.286, and dividing this percentage in the same ratio as the enlistments for British Columbia bear to those for the Yukon (that is to say as 51,430 is to 2,327) gives for British Columbia 9.841 per cent and for the Yukon .445 per cent.
I notice that the percentages in the resolution now before the House differ from those as quoted in the bill last year, and probably there is some good reason for that. But they do differ. Apparently the percentages given in the bill and in the Ralston report were not correct, otherwise they would not be changed this year; and taking it on this y ear's percentage the calculation for Yukon will be somewhat different. The percentage for British Columbia and Yukon this year, instead of 10.286 per cent is now 11.213 per cent, and calculated on that basis the Yukon percentage should be .503, or about $11,000 in money. A'fter getting the information from Colonel Ralston I corresponded with the officials of the Dawson branch of the Great War Veterans' Association, submitting the whole question to them for suggestions. I have here a letter from the secretary-treasurer of that institution to the following effect:
Dear Sir,-The Dawson Branch G.W.V.A. have instructed me to thank you for communications regarding the canteen fund.
The enclosed copies of a resolution passed at a largely attended meeting of the branch along with a number of other returned men expresses the unanimous and emphatic opinion of all present.
This matter has further been discussed with a number of prominent citizens including Mr. Percy Reid, Acting Gold Commissioner, and all seem to hold the same opinion as we do.
Canteen Funds

The resolution of the Great War Veterans' Association reads:
Resolved, that notwithstanding the disadvantage to which the Yukon is put through having no percentage of discharges or pensions taken into consideration in arriving at the sum aJlotable to the Territory from the canteen fund, this meeting nevertheless, with a view to arriving at a practical and expeditious solution of the difficulty, acquiesce in the figure of .445 per cent of the whole quoted by Mt. Ralston, Chairman of the Royal Commission on Pensions and Reestablishment, in his letters to Captain George Black, federal member of parliament for the Yukon, such percentage being based on enlistments only and amounting at present to $10,242, as being reasonably satisfactory under the circumstances.
Be it further resolved, that, due to the isolated position of the Yukon Territory, the lack of adequate communication during the greater part of the year, and the absolute impossibility of a committee situate 2,000 miles from here being able to handle the local situation sympathetically or intelligently, this meeting is of the opinion that it is in the best interests of Yukon residents entitled to receive benefits under the canteen fund that the Yukon's pro rata share of .445 per cent of the whole be handled by a local committee and that the Gold Commissioner and Captain George Black, federal member of parliament, be requested to give every assistance with that object in view.
That is signed by the president and the secretary. On February 24 this year I wrote to the minister enclosing a copy of that resolution. I will not take the time of the House reading my letter but I should like to put it on Hansard in order to make clear my position in regard to the matter. The letter was dated Ottawa, February 24, addressed to the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment.

re Canteen Fund
