On the basis of calculation used in arriving at the sums to be allotted to the various provinces Yukon would be entitled to .445 of the whole, and amounting to at present $10,242 such percentage being based on nnlistments only and not including pensions and discharges.
I enclose, herewith, an original copy of resolution passed at a representative meeting of the G.W.V.A. and other returned soldiers held at Dawson, January 14, 1925, in which it is declared that it would be more satisfactory to have the Yukon's share of the fund handled by a local committee than to have the same combined with that of British Columbia. I was disappointed at receiving on February 27 the following letter in reply:
Dear Captain Black,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 24th instant with reference to the distribution of the Yukon's share of tfie canteen funds.
The change which is suggested would entail the making-up of a new scale for the whole country, and moreover the other provinces might submit that discrimination had been shown against them inasmuch as a different basis for computing the Yukon's share would have to be used.
It is difficult to see how this can be justified.
As I stated at the outset, I am glad' to find that the minister has modified that opinion and told the House that if the committee favours it he will be willing to allow an alteration in the bill to provide that the Yukon share may be placed in the hands of a local committee. I would therefore suggest for the consideration of the minister the following amendment:
That the resolution be amended by adding after the word " provincial " in the fourth paragraph the words " and territorial " and by striking out the word " nine " and substituting the word '" ten " in paragraph (4) and that the British Columbia proportion be 10.710 and the Yukon ipro-portion .503 instead of the proportions now in the resolution stated; and that a new paragraph be added as-
(5) (a) The Yukon allotment to be paid to a board of trustees consisting of the Gold Commissioner of Yukon and the president and secretary of the Dawson branch of Great War Veterans' Association, withoi-.t remuneration, empowered to receive and hold the territorial allotment and to ascertain the wishes of those interested and residing in the territory concerning the disposition of such allotment, and to determine the object to which the allotment should be devoted, and to administer the same for such object or to provide for such administration by others. The expenses in conneetion with the trust to be a charge on the allotment.
I am quite sure the charges on the allotment will not amount to anything. The figures are based on the information I received from Colonel Ralston, the chairman of the Ralston commission, giving the method of calculating these percentages and amending them in accordance with the figures now given in the resolution, which as I pointed out before differ from the percentages given in the bill last year. be a fair basis of calculation, and I would be very willing indeed' to have it adopted. As to the other clauses of the resolution and of the bill of last year, they did not pass without protest, at any rate on my part. After the splendid work done by the returned soldiers through their organizations and agencies had been discussed in the House, I said:
If the work has been done so well in the past why create another agency now?
That was in reference to this proposed adjustment service and bureau.
Surely the efforts of returned soldiers on their own behalf, coupled with the work done by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, ought to be sufficient, but if an additional bureau is needed, I submit that the expense should not be met by withdrawing $100,000 from the canteen fund. That should be a government expense coming on the whole people. This $100,000 is not a gift to the returned soldiers in fact the whole of this $2,296,936 is the returned soldiers' own money now. It does not belong to the government or to the general public, it belongs to the returned men, who overseas ran a canteen and made a profit out of it, and now the money is their own.
I submit that neither the $100,000 or any other sum should be taken out for this purpose. The bureau, according to the minister's own words is not necessary because the soldiers' interests are being so well looked after by the government and by the soldiers themselves.
I quote that to show the minister was not altogether correct in saying the legislation passed without protest; and to-night we have heard pro-tests from many returned soldiers' organizations read by members of the House. With all due deference to the minister, I do not think he has been quite frank with the House or with the committee in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In what way may I ask?

As I say, with all due deference to the minister, I think at the outset he sought to make it appear that no payments had been made or were contemplated to be made from the canteen fund to the Dominion Veterans' Alliance. He was asked on February 26 and 27, and again on March 5, if an order in council allocating any part of this canteen fund to the Dominion Veterans' Alliance had been passed, and the answer was in the negative.

speechtext: That was strictly true.

Oh, perhaps in the letter, but not by any means in the spirit. It was only when an hon. member produced a co-py of the order in council and read it that the minister admitted there was any order in council at all. No one can read that order in council without realizing from it that money to the extent of $15,000, perhaps $25,000, has already been expended in anticipation of this $100,000, 'and apparently the minister is going to see to it that the trustees, whoever they may be, undertake to return that $15,000 or $25,000, whichever it is, to the soldiers' disablement fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
If they do not think the money has been properly expended for the maintenance of the bureau, they may refuse to reimburse1 the disablement fund, and the situation will be that the disablement fund will have improperly contributed to the maintenance of the bureau during a year and a half or two years.
Canteen Funds

I think the minister is going to know his trustees pretty well before they are appointed, and if they are not prepared to do as he thinks they should do they are not apt to be appointed. The order in council in fact had been issued many months before hon. members in this House directed this question to the minister. An order in council was issued and $25,000 of the disablement fund was used.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

speechtext:
I submit it is fair to suppose from reading the order in council which finally came to light that these trustees are practically to be directed to take that amount out of the canteen fund and pay it over to the disablement fund. These are the words of the minister, in fact of the government, in the order in council:
-and he recommends that the trustees who may be appointed after the passage of the Canteen Funds Bill at the next session of parliament be requested to reimburse the disablement fund the amount of $15,000 out of any moneys transferred to such trustees undsr the authority of the said bill.
That, to say the least, is a pretty straight tip to those trustees before they are appointed as to what they are expected to do. I cannot satisfy myself from the wording of the order in council whether the amount advanced was $15,000 or $25,000. There are two amounts of $10,000 and one of $5,000 mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I said to my hon. friend it is $15,000, and I wish he would accept my word.
I did not understand that before. The minister's word is clearer than the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I admit that the wording is a little ambiguous.

I say, as I said
last session, that this adjustment service and bureau, such as is contemplated by the resolution, is unnecessary, and if it is not unnecessary it ought to be unnecessary. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is after all an adjustment service and bureau. It is a soldiers' bureau, or it should be. If it is not, what is it? What was it designed for? It is not needed in the general government of this country. We had sufficient departments to carry on the government of Canada, perhaps a few too many, before the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment was ever thought of, and it was created simply because services of that sort were necessary for the returned soldiers. 
If the department is not an adjustment bureau, a soldiers' service bureau-well, what is the minister doing? What is the reason for his continuance in office if that is not what the department is for? And what is the large and expensive staff of the department being maintained for if it does not constitute a soldiers' bureau, if it is not for the purpose of attending to the business of returned soldiers? I submit that it is an admission of incompetence on the part of the 10 pun. department and of the head of the department to say that any go-between, any special agency is necessary as a medium of intercourse between his department and the returned soldiers. The soldiers should not require special counsel; the members of the minister's staff ought to be special counsel to every man who has to do business with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend is sliding into politics.

Well, I do not
know that the members of the government have always been unwilling to bring politics into matters affecting the soldiers. Friends of his party did what they could in the constituencies during the by-elections to inflame the returned soldiers against the Conservative party in the account they gave to the public of how the pension bill of last session was handled. Right here let me call attention to a very refreshing sentence in this order in council. Let me quote the words:
Owing to the fact that this measure was introduced during the last few days of the parliamentary session, it failed to become law.
Now that is a plain statement of fact, and it differs very widely from the statement I heard made in the constituencies during the elections last fall as to why that bill failed to pass. Every effort was made, as I say, to prejudice the returned soldiers against the Conservative party because the pension bill of last session failed to pass-owing, the government's canvassers said, to the antagonism of the Conservative majority in the Senate. Though if we look at the history of the respective parties we will find that returned soldiers and soldiers before they returned fared quite as well at the hands of the Conservative party as they did at the hands of my hon. friends opposite. If we are going to talk politics in connection with this matter I am quite willing to do so.
We have had complaints, and we are getting them right along, from returned soldiers all over the country as to the policy of the pension board and the Department of Soldiers'

Canteen Funds
Civil Re-establishment. The policy of the pension, board and the policy of the department are .just exactly what the minister makes them; the pension board, like government officials in other departments, take their lead from the minister. If the policy of the pension board was not to the liking of the minister it would very soon be changed. I say that if such an adjustment sendee and bureau is needed, let the public pay for it. We heard a lot about the gratitude of the public to the returned soldiers when they were overseas, and I do not think the great majority of the civilian population, taxpayers of this country, would be at all averse to putting up $100,000 if that amount were needed to give the soldiers the benefit of special counsel here at the capital-because that is what the taking of this $100,000 means. On the other hand, if there must be such an "adjustment service and bureau," as it is expressed in the resolution, and at the expense of the canteen fund, I say, put that fund in the hands of independent trustees, not trustees who will take orders from the minister, no matter how fair or how proper those orders may be. The trustees should be absolutely free and untrammelled; they should not be handicapped in any way. As I have already pointed out, this order in council indicates all too plainly that they will get orders, if they do not get orders they will get directions. They are going to get advice as to what they are to do with $15,000 of this fund, to start with. That is not the sort of trustees we want. Let me say, with all respect to members of this House and officers of the permanent force or the Canadian corps, that in selecting these trustees the government might very well consider the advisability of including among them one or two who perhaps are not generals in the army. I heard to-day nothing but the names of generals suggested. I have every respect for these gentlemen, for their rank and their military records; but I do say that in civilian life to-day are to be found men who never wore a brass hat, who never obtained the rank of an officer, yet who have the entire respect of the community in which they live, have a wide circle of acquaintance, and would be quite fit and proper persons to be on that board of trustees.

May I ask my hon. friend one question as a matter of information? I did not hear more than one general mentioned, and that was Sir Arthur Currie. Were there
some others?

There were at least three others. I would rather not repeat their names; you will find it in Hansard to-morrow.
I say it would be better to leave the $100,000 in the hands of the minister and allow him and his government to take the responsibility for the administration of this fund than to shift the responsibility to trustees who are not absolutely independent.
If the minister is bound to use this $100,000, and I suppose he is, for the establishment of this bureau, then let him safeguard it by the terms of the bill so that it will not be sloughed off or frittered away. So word the bill that in the first place the fund will not be plundered of that S15,000. That $15,000 should never go out of the canteen fund to the disablement fund. We heard it said with some heat on the floor of this House by gentlemen opposite on the last occasion on which this resolution was discussed that it was entirely proper to use the disablement fund to the extent of $15,000 for the purpose for which it was used. If that is so, let it go at that, write it off. There is no reason why it should be paid back from this canteen fund; and that is one thing that should be safeguarded by the terms of the bill. I would provide for the investment of this $100,000 so that the bureau could be maintained indefinitely by the interest earned by that sum. I do not see any necessity for establishing any very elaborate bureau or agency service here at the capital. One smart agent ought to be quite enough; this $100,000 should earn $5,000 a year, and you could get a good enough man for $5,000. It follows as a matter of course that the great majority of cases could be handled without the intervention of this agency at all. Only a few contentious cases will come before the bureau. We have a corps of paid soldiers' advocates across the country from Halifax to Vancouver, paid by the month I understand; they might do a little for the soldiers in return for their salaries. I say it could only and should only be a very exceptional case that this bureau would have to handle, and an agent of ordinary intelligence, with the co-operation of the minister and his staff, should be quite sufficient to handle the business. Therefore I say that the bill should provide that the principal amount of $100,000 be invested and that the bureau be conducted on the interest earned thereon. I do not want to be misunderstood: I am entirely opposed to the use of this $100,000 for the purpose proposed. But if the minister must have his way and must put it through, put it through with those safeguards. Although attention has already been called to this feature of the resolution reserving the sum of $20,000 for the payment of any outstanding accounts, I cannot bring myself to believe that any such amount of

speechtext: I do not say exactly what I shall do in this connection. This is a most unusual .procedure. I rise not for the purpose of opposing this resolution, but to give it my support. This is a very old question, one which has been before the eyes and attention of returned men and others for a number of years. Nevertheless, in giving it my support, I fear it is not going to solve the difficulties of an adjustment bureau. Let us go back a few years to the after period of the war. Immediately after the war ended, adjustment bureaus, committees, and associations were formed throughout the Dominion of Canada to take up the various questions of returned men, and to do the best they could for them, their widows and orphans. These adjustment bureaus have laboured under many adverse conditions, but they have been able to accomplish a great deal. My experience has been that the function of these adjustment bureaus has been to adjust cases so far as they were able to do so, and in this regard they have fulfilled as far as possible their duties to returned men, the different representative bodies and the country.
Clause 2 of the resolution states that the sum of $1CO,000 is to be paid to a central board of three trustees for the purpose of maintaining an adjustment service and bureau for the benefit of ex-service 'men and their dependents. What would be the function of that bureau? I would gather that it would be similar to that of the different organizations that were formed in the past. 1 have always believed that it is the responsibility of the state and that it should never have been the responsibility of organizations of returned men to contribute to an adjustment bureau or service organization to bring forward their different needs and requirements. I am convinced that the question of giving to returned men, their widows and orphans their just dues and rights is a responsibility of the federal government. If we had had a department or a branch of a department in which the returned men had absolute confidence, it would not be necessary now to finance an adjustment bureau by the returned men or from the canteen fund. It is the duty of the state to give the leturned men what is their due without their being obliged to put up a continual fight such as we have witnessed throughout the length and breadth of the country. It has been brought to the attention of parliament and of every government that has been in power since the war that the returned men

Canteen Funds

have had to finance their own organizations in order to obtain what has been regarded as their just due, and in that way it seems to me that the responsibility of the state has been shifted in the administration of some of our departments. In establishing another adjustment bureau we are only perpetuating a good deal of the dissatisfaction that now prevails. Nevertheless, it is my opinion that the bureau is absolutely necessary; I am not of the opinion that it can be done without. I will go so far as to say however that there should have been no necessity for it; it has been my candid opinion that the bureau should have been unnecessary, and we should not have had to pass legislation of this kind, taking money from the canteen funds that belongs to the returned1 men who enlisted and using it for the purpose of financing this institution.
On the other hand, in face of the conditions that exist, I am quite willing to support ithe resolution. From my experience gathered in the past few years in which I have been a member of the special committee investigating pensions and matters of re-establishment, I have come to the conclusion that something was necessary. It has been brought to the attention of parliament that there was a necessity for something in the shape of an investigation, and a commission was appointed, known as the Ralston commission, who after a thorough inquiry brought in a report recommending that steps be taken to provide funds for an adjustment service. I feel therefore that the bureau is necessary, and the next move is to provide the funds. I mulst frankly say however that I cannot agree that it is the duty of returned men's organizations to take their own funds to finance their adjustment service and bureau. I should think that the country would be of the opinion that these organizations deserve some contribution from the general funds to the extent of one hundred, or one hundred and fifty, or two hundred thousand dollars. In view of what is taking place, in view of the different investigations that have been held, I feel that the present is the next best move; but as I have stated before, it is my opinion that if the country had had confidence in the different tribunals that have been set up, this legislation would have been unnecessary.
Now, I do not wish to have it inferred from anything I have said, nor do I want it insinuated, that it is my desire to drag polities into this question in any way whatever, but I feel that I am bound to take this stand in view of all the circumstances. And I take it without prejudice and absolutely with no

desire to reflect upon any of the administrators of the departments. The fact however is, it seems to me, that had the returned men and their organizations had confidence in the Board of Pension Commissioners, and had that body functioned in such a way as to overcome many of the difficulties that arise to-day, as they have arisen in the past few years, the present undertaking would have been obviated. What would be said if during the present session legislation were introduced to establish an adjustment bureau to take care of claims coming before the Civil Service Commission, or an adjustment bureau in connection with the Board of Railway Commissioners? Well, as I see it, the Board of Pension Commissioners is to some extent in the same category as the railway commission or the Civil Service Commission. Here we are providing machinery to enable the returned men to secure their just due, when there Should be no necessity at all for it. It has been proved to my satisfaction that within the past four years particularly the vast majority of these cases have been adjusted by representatives of the organizations before the Board of Pension Commissioners, and I reiterate that if the Board of Pension Commissioners had functioned as the people believed it should have done this legislation would now be uncalled for. Under the circumstances, however, I am perfectly satisfied that this legislation is absolutely in the best interests of the returned men, especially in view of the thorough survey carried out by the Ralston commission. And so far as I have been able to ascertain it has the unanimous approval of the returned men. I am sure that there may be some objections to this legislation, but in view of all the conditions I feel that I can give it my hearty support as being in the very best interests of the returned men and of the country as a whole.

An afternoon and evening spent in this way in friendly debate in the interests of the returned men is well spent. As I have stated before, some of the men have sent telegrams on this question and I find that there is a great deal of objection to this particular division. The minister will remember that we had a Red Cross and a patriotic fund, involving some $44,000,000, the administration of which was carried out by a large number of prominent business men throughout Canada at a minimum of cost. Here is a canteen fund of about two and a quarter millions and I think it will be agreed that in these four or five sections of the resolution we have the costliest piece of adminia-

Canteen Funds
tration provided for. It is a waste of money, and after the various administrators, Dominion and provincial have got through, there will be very little left to be devoted to the objects of the Ralston report. Here we are in 1925 seven years after the war providing for an adjustment bureau with headquarters at Ottawa and with a paid staff. What it is necessary for I do not know, for I cannot see what it will adjust. I thought that one first result of the Ralston commission's inquiry would be the simplifying of the Pension Act; but there is such a vast amount of red tape connected with the whole thing that the functions of the central board have been largely frustrated. I fail to see what good this particular board can do in the case of a soldier living in London, in Hamilton or in St. Catharines. What is there to adjust?
Why should a soldier need somebody to fight his case for his pension with the government- seven years after the war? Why should we have to go before the D.S.C.R., the pension board, the Federal appeal board, this new bureau, the Soldiers' Aid Commission of Ontario, the municipality, the local soldiers' organizations, and the unit to which he belongs? Why all this red tape seven years after the war to get a small claim against the government adjusted? The soldier is not going to live forever; these returned men are dying off by hundreds every month. Here you have a canteen fund of two and a half million dollars to administer, and you have a complex system of red tape with five or six methods of disposing of it. In the c-ase of the $45,000,000 patriotic fund the services of some of our prominent business men in Canada were enlisted free and the fund was administered with a minimum of cost to the country and the maximum of efficiency.
I think the minister would have been well advised if he had followed a similar course for the administration of the $2,250,000 canteen funds. And I hope he will not think any remarks made from this side of the House are made in an unfriendly way, because I am sure all three parties in the House are trying to do the best they can to help the minister and our returned men. One of the objects of forming the DiS.C.R., as I understand, was largely on account of the lack of sympathy and the red tape in the Militia department. It was felt that that department had not full sympathy with the returned men in some resipects, although it gave a good account of itself during and after the war.
This so called central bureau is claiming for itself very large functions and powers-for the 97i
maintenance and assistance of ex-service men and their dependents. It will not do the work at all. Evidently that is the view of the provincial government of Ontario, for, acting on the report of the Ralston commission, they have voted, I think, $50,000 for the purpose of aiding the returned men of Ontario in presenting their applications before the Dominion government for pensions and relief. Therefore in my opinion, Mr. Chairman, any necessity for the establishment of this proposed bureau is largely taken away by the action of the Ontario government and of various local organizations of returned men who assist the returned soldier to present his case.
I notice that the sum of $20,000 is to be held for the payment of any outstanding accounts. That should never have been charged to this fund; it should have been looked after by the D.S.C.R. Why should a returned man seven years after the war have to retain a lawyer to get his rights which the people of Canada and this parliament are anxious that he should get? No narrow technical construction is now placed upon the Pension Act, and in my opinion there is no occasion for distributing the canteen funds in this way. I agree with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) that instead of allocating $100,000 to a central board, the work which this central board is to look after should be attended to by the Soldiers Civil Re-establishment department of the government. Indeed, I have every confidence that the minister himself would do far better work with this $100,000 than a central bureau of irresponsible people having no connection with the government and not accountable to the soldiers. As to the provincial boards to be appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council in each province, I fail to see what use such boards will be to the returned men. Last year when this matter was up the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Manion) asked what the duties of the readjustment board would be, and the minister (Mr. Beland) quoting from the Ralston report, said:
There are a variety of instances in connection with such questions as government employment, land settlement, training, housing and rehabilitation activities generally, the considerations affecting which depend on the presentation of the individual case rather than on the terms of a general regulation. There are also parliamentary matters not only affecting pensions but amendments to existing statutes which may indirectly affect the rights and privileges of ex-service men, and in addition there is the desirability of having some agency completely detached from government organization to supply the necessary personal contact between ex-service men and dependents and those who deal with matters affecting their interests.
And he added:
Canteen Funds

This outline fully indicates what the duties of the service bureau will be and, I think, are, because at the present time those duties are being discharged here in Ottawa, and in my opinion to the general satisfaction of the men.
Well, as I have already said, the government of Ontario have offered to fight the cases of returned men before the appeal board, and with the new Pension Act provisions. There should not be any necessity for bureaus and a lot of organizations to get a returned man justice and his rights without all this trouble and annoyance.
The third clause proposes that $50,000 shall be paid to the United Services fund of Great Britain, and $50,000 to the American Red Cross. In my opinion any of our returned men in distress in the United States should be repatriated by the government of Canada and civilly re-established here. Many of them cannot get work there because they will not take out naturalization papers. After the Civil War the Grand Army of the Republic did not have to leave the United States to look for work; they found ample opportunities for their abilities and energies in their own country and members of which organization became President of the United States, state governors, presidents of railways, and filled other important executive positions all over the country, with the result that they dominated public life and the government of the United States for fifty years after Lee's surrender to Grant and the civil war of the North and South was ended. They got into politics and stayed there and the returned men in Canada should follow their noble .example.
Rather than create a control board it would be better if the minister and his department did this work themselves. It was [DOT]stated by the minister last year that the residue of the fund was quite a respectable sum, amounting to over $2,000,000. This, he said, was to be divided among the nine provinces on a pro rata basis. The Lieutenant Governor in Council in each province was to appoint a board to administer the fund. The minister was asked whether any ballot had been taken to ascertain the views of the returned men, and he replied that 5,000 ballots had been cast by returned men and that the largest number of votes was given in favour of the education of orphan children;-schemes of education, and that the second largest favoured relieving meritorious cases or cases of unemployment and distress. These were the two main schemes -suggested. If it is a question of relieving meritorious
11 p.m. cases and cases of unemployment, this money could far better be 
distributed among the municipalities throughout the country for that purpose.
The Ralston commission went into the whole question of the canteen fund. They investigated what the Mother Country had done and what methods had been adopted in Australia and the United States, and they made certain recommendations. The first principle the adoption of which the commission recommended was as follows:
Firstly, that the fund should, in the opinion of the commission, not be sipent immediately but its use should be providently spread over a reasonable number of years so that there would be something available for children now very young who might later be benefited by special assistance in particularly distressing circumstances which might arise at any time* until a wage-earning period is reached, or who might become eligible for school or university scholarships It such were created. Neither should the fund be kept perpetually.
I think that is a good principle. The report continues:
The report of the United Services fund in Great Britain contains the .following:-
"It is preferable in a fund of this nature that the greatest amount of good should be done over a limited period of reasonable length rather than that any sum should be set aside for an indefinite period.*' In England the period decided on was fifteen years from 1923.
Then the other recommendations they make are as follows:
Secondly, any use of the fund for relief purposes from time to time should be limited to the class of cases for which no relief is then available from government sources; in other words, the money should not be used to relieve the state of any responsibil.ty devolving on it.
I think that is a good principle, because many returned men who were over in France for two, three or four years get no relief under existing legislation. Such a fund as this would take care of some of these cases.
Thirdly, that only ex-members of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces below commissioned rank who served in France or England, and their dependents, should be eligible to participate in the benefits of the fund.
That is to give the rank and file the benefit of the fund; I think that is a very wise proviso. With these principles in mind -the commission has two suggestions to make regarding schemes for disposition of the fund, as follows:
(a)	Assistance to specially meritorious cases where ex-members of the forces and their dependents are n genuine distress. No elaboration is needed here. The experience of the United Services fund of Great Britain will afford valuable information and guidance. This is the purpose for which a similar fund is used in Australia, and has been frequently put forward as a suggestion.
(b)	The provision of scholarships in schools (not necessarily confined to the higher grades) and universities, for specially promising children of ex-servwa men.

Canteen Funds
With regard to that educational clause, many children whose fathers were killed in the war can only with difficulty be sent to high school on the miserable pittance of $18 a month given for maintenance of high school children.
The main recommendation of the Ralston report is in respect to meritorious cases or cases of unemployment. Just the other day the Mayor of Brantford sent a communication to Ottawa addressed to the Prime Minister, in which he said:
Situation, among unemployed ex-service men and their families one of extreme seriousness. Local organizations, churches and municipal authorities doing everything possible to provide relief among the unemployed. We respectfully suggest that men who served overseas and their dependents have special right to look to federal government of Canada with reasonable confidence for asistance in such period of difficulty and distress. May we urge cabinet consideration.
The hon. member for Kingston said that returned men who were out of work were the wards of the state, and so they are. They should be and they are entitled to be looked after properly. They should not be obliged to go around the large cities, when they are out of work, begging for relief for themselves and their families. I believe the minister tried to do what he could last year in this connection, but all the government can do is a mere nothing when you consider the large number of men who are in need of assistance. I say again that either the minister should take charge of this fund himself or he should appoint two or three good business men, such as those who gave their services in connection with the patriotic fund and red cross activities, to administer the fund. If that was done a great deal of unnecessary and useless duplication and paid organization would be saved and a great deal of unnecessary work and red tape would be avoided.

Mr. Chairman, it is
eleven o'clock, and I think we-
Go on.
We will go on if you wish, but I was going to suggest to the minister that there are a number of members who wish to take some part in this discussion.
Bring them here.

I refer to such members as the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) an outstanding returned soldier member of this House, who has always been on the committees dealing with these matters and who is well posted on them. The reason he is not here is because none of us expected that this matter was to come up to-day. Until
I got here this afternoon I had no idea that the resolution was to be taken up; I thought it was likely to go over until after the budget debate. There is no intention of holding the minister up, but I would like to point out to him, as I said to him privately a moment ago, that whatever time is taken up now on the resolution will be saved when the bill is before the House. I would ask the minister to let the resolution stand over for another day, if reasonably assured that it will not be further held up; I know of no reason why it should not carry the next time it is considered. There are quite a number of points about this resolution which we have not yet dealt with. I was going to speak just two hours ago on one aspect of the case; I was going to bring to the attention of the minister again the question of the $100,000, but I was interrupted, I think b}^ the hon. member for Yukon; some others followed him, and I have not since had a chance to say a word. I do not wish to go on at this stage.
Go on.

That is for the minister
to say; if he says so, we will go on. I think, however, he will not save any particular time by going on. He would probably be just as well advised to have the resolution held up another day.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We discussed the resolution on a former occasion for two hours, and we have discussed it the whole of to-day with the exception of the hour given to the budget. Apparently only one clause of the resolution lends itself to objection on the part of certain hon. members. I think that almost every hon. member who has an interest in this resolution has addressed the House. The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) for whom I have the greatest admiration, was in his seat the other day and shared in the discussion. I say in reply to my hon. friend that if he is willing to allow the resolution to pass, we will introduce the bill this evening, and it will go down on the order paper for its Second reading, and then the next time the bill comes up in the House there will be ample opportunity for discussion on the second reading, and again in committee of the Whole, when the whole bill will have to be considered clause by clause, and when any amendment may be proposed. I have supplied the House with a'll possible information in connection with this measure. It passed the House last year, and hon. members are perfectly conversant with the whole situation. I think the House has been given
Canteen Funds

the most generous treatment in connection with this bill. Now I appeal to my hon. friend to allow this resolution to pass. That does not commit him or his friends in any degree.

I am sorry to disagree with my -hon. friend, but it does commit us. The resolution when passed absolutely commits us to the principles and there are two or three principles which I wish to discuss before agreeing with them. I have no intention at the present time of pressing some of the objections which I, and I think other hon. members, have to a vote, but we wish to discuss the resolution fairly before it passes. I do not wish to reply to the minister until he has finished his remarks, but I would ask him to bear in mind that if we vote for the resolution, we are voting for the principles of the resolution, and with some of them we do not agree at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I take it for granted that
my hon. friend agrees to the principle of the resolution.

The large principle, but
not with smaller principles.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants
to have clauses of the bill amended, it will be open to him to move an amendment in committee of the Whole on the bill. I appeal to my hon. friend. I think in the interests of expedition of business in this House it will be better to allow this resolution to pass tonight. I think we have been most generous in regard to this measure, and if we allowed as much time on every other measure as we have allowed for discussion on this, the session would never come to an end.

I would like to point this out to the minister. While it is quite true this discussion was introduced this afternoon after the budget speech was delivered, though I have a vital interest in this matter, I have been on my feet only twice since the budget speech was delivered, and each time it was merely to ask the minister a question, I have some rather extended observations to make first, on clause 2 of the resolution. There are several things that I do not agree with, and perhaps the minister knows my position on that clause fairly well from my questions. Again, clause 5, which refers to the whole fund, involving an amount of $2,000,000, has not had one word of discussion. I want to tell the minister now that I do not agree with the principle of his resolution, and before the bill is introduced I would like to have the opportunity of presenting my posi-*Mr. Beland.]
tion to the House. There has been no objection taken by any member so far in regard to the principle involved in clause 5, which relates to the disposal of $2,000,000, and I do not think it is fair to ask any hon. member to make a presentation in regard to the principle of a clause involving the disposal of $2,000,000 at ten minutes after eleven.
Why?

Would it be fair to ask
any minister to commence the discussion of any subject after eleven o'clock at night? Why not bring down the budget after eleven o'clock, and then go on with the budget debate? I am pointing out that there has not been one word of debate on clause 5 this afternoon or evening, and I assure the minister that it is perhaps the mo'st vital portion of his resolution. Personally I have not been given one opportunity to speak on any portion of this resolution since it was introduced this afternoon. I have asked two or three questions but I certainly have not made any remarks on the resolution, because I have not had the opportunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend in a
position to say how much longer time he would require, he and his friends, to dispose of the resolution or come to a vote on it?
So far as I am concerned, I would certainly want three-quarters of an hour.
Go ahead.

I assure the minister that
the observations I will make will require some further discussion. I know there will be points brought out that certainly members on this side of the House will want to discuss, and I am quite certain that if hon. members opposite whom I now see thick in their seats, but who took no interest in this debate this afternoon and this evening-
We are having enough now.

Hon. members are interrupting me now when I am attempting to present the matter in fairness to the minister. All I am asking is fair treatment, for an opportunity to discuss the disposal of the main portion of the canteen fund, involving $2,000,000, and which portion of the resolution has not received five minutes of discussion either to-day or at any time this year.

Before the minister replies, may I say further that my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) is not the only one

Canteen Funds
[DOT]who wishes to discuss this matter? The minister asked the hon. member for Burrard how long he would be likely to take, and the hon. member has indicated how long he would take. I have already suggested to the minister, and I repeat it, that I have no reason for believing that there would be any likelihood of holding this bill up further than possibly another afternoon. That means only three hours, and possibly part of the evening at most, of another day. The discussion that takes place on the resolution will mean that much less discussion on the bill, because we will have come to an agreement, I hope, with the minister. I am not criticizing the minister's attitude this afternoon in any way. He has been quite reasonable in his acceptance of suggestions that have been put forward, and I give him credit for that. There are other questions upon which, if we had more time, he would perhaps come to agree with us. I again suggest to the minister, and I make this suggestion just as much for the purpose of saving time as my hon. friend the minister desires it, that he hold this over for another day and discuss it on one more occasion, whenever he wishes; that is his privilege, of course. The discussion that takes place on the resolution will save time on the bill.

Just before the minister answers, we all know what took place in this House in regard to this legislation on a previous occasion. This House has been accused of not sending legislation forward early enough, and it seems to me that with all the discussion we have had, we really ought to be in a position to get down to some basis of co-operation, and advance some legislation. It would appear to me that there would be ample opportunity for making suggestions or even amendments when the bill comes down and is considered clause by clause in committee. I would be strongly in favour of asking the minister to go on with the resolution.

the government plant now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has control of it at the moment, yes.

Did the department
carry its investigation far enough to satisfy itself that peat can be manufactured at a marketable price?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, within a reasonable shipping distance.
To compete with coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In view of the discontinuance of its own experiments, is the government rendering any assistance to those who are still making tests? I have in mind a man in western Ontario who has been engaged in this work for at least fifteen years and at various times he has put a considerable quantity of the product on the market, having spent a lot of money in connection with the manufacturing of peat. This plant is located in the county of Middlesex near London. I wonder whether the government renders any assistance in a case of that kind where private individuals are conducting experiments on their own behalf. The briquettes placed on the market from this source have given very general satisfaction, but it seems a considerable undertaking for a private individual, as in this case, to carry on experiments of that kind over a number of years without receiving some assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are alwaj'S ready to lend any assistance we can. There is an engineer in the city who thinks we are on the wrong track with our process, which is one of sun-drying; he thinks it is possible to squeeze the moisture out of peat by pressure. So far as we are able to discover, in Germany, in Great Britain and elsewhere, that process has never been successful although it would be very desirable if it were practicable. However, we have
given him material to go on with in his experiments to see whether be can demonstrate the possibility of separating by pressure the fuel from the water content. I cannot say what success he has had. As to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. 'Sutherland), I 'have never heard of the gentleman to whom he has referred; at any rate, be has not applied to the department, so far as we know. Ontario is of course one of the acute fuel areas in Canada and there is an immense amount of peat in the province; so that if this peat can be manufactured by a perfected process we are certainly very much interested in the possibility.

Has not the pressure
process been attempted in this country? I remember twenty-five years ago inspecting a plant in Toronto where they were attempting to eliminate the moisture by pressure. They spent many thousands of dollars without any result.

It was a pressure
process that was applied in the plant I have referred to. Of course, the peat is dried as much as possible before it is subjected to treatment and I know that the operator had great confidence in being eventually successful. During the past two years I have heard nothing further than that he was carrying on. I visited the plant at one time and was much interested in it; I was particularly impressed with the owner's confidence in his ability to make a success of it. I must say I was somewhat disappointed to learn that the government had almost given up hopes of being successful with the experiments carried on in the vicinity of Ottawa. The fuel question is of great importance to this country and every encouragement should be given in a case such as that to which I 'have referred, if any encouragement can be given by the government, for it would mean a great deal to the people of that locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is it partly a pressure process?

Yes, very largely,
and the plant is considerable. The owner is Dr. Williams of London. He at one time resided in a place close by and acquired the property, and he has since spent a large amount of money developing the plant in the township of Dorchester.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Apparently the briquetting money spent did not result in very much.

speechtext:
At Bienfait?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes. As I understand,
the process which the government developed did not prove practical when applied to large quantities of peat.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, yes it
is quite practical. There is the question perhaps of expense, but there is no question about the practicability of the process.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It was not commercially practicable. The process finally adopted was that in use in the States. This is not very encouraging for our research work, and it looks as if we would get along better if we just watched what other people were doing. Now the whole thing is taken over by Mr. Hugh Sutherland. If he is the man I take him to be, he is approximately 80 or 82 years of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He is the
head of the company.

I wish him success. I
find in all these departments a list of officials that really makes one quail to read, but the Department of Mines has all the belts and records for strange names. I do not suppose any of us know anything about them, and I should 'like to have some of the officials produced to see what they look like. For instance, here is an archaeologist, followed by a zoologist (mammalia), an ornithologist, a chief botanist, several ethnologists, an associate invertebrate palaeontologist. Then there is a head translator. One is at a loss to know what he can be translating.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is translating for our French editions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know what he
needs to be translating into French or English either in the Mines department. Then we have a peat specialist still, although the peat work is done; next we have a chief taxidermist and herpetologist, a cartographer, an artist in vertebrate palaeontology and two assistant artists, an assistant ethnologist, two collector preparator specialists, an assistant invertebrate palaiontologist, three senior collector preparators, and so on. Who is the real author of these names? I have not mentioned the herbarium assistant. Several officials have left the department I know, but it does 
really look as though there were a lot of men engaged in doing something which does not seem to me to be connected with mineralogy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Quite true; all those strange names come from the museum.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is where they ought to be.
